The Two Welfare Theorems

Walk along the utility possibility frontier. Pick a point with the slider and move it around.

The competitive equilibrium always sits on the frontier. That is the First Welfare Theorem. Other points on the frontier are reachable too. Support the point with the right price and shift income in one lump sum. Then the market lands there by itself. That is the Second Theorem, and the formula below gives the transfer.

For example, say you and a 🧑 friend split 10 🍬 candies. Every split that uses all 10 is efficient. But if your friend's share feels too small, there is a fix. Hand a few candies to your friend before trading starts. Then plain market trading reaches the split you wanted.

(u1,u2) on the frontier  ⟺  Pareto efficient(u_1, u_2) \text{ on the frontier} \iff \text{Pareto efficient}(u1​,u2​) on the frontier⟺Pareto efficient
T=p⋅(x1−e1)(lump-sum transfer)T = p \cdot (x^1 - e^1) \quad \text{(lump-sum transfer)}T=p⋅(x1−e1)(lump-sum transfer)

Both marginal rates of substitution equal the equilibrium price p1/p2=1p_1/p_2 = 1p1​/p2​=1, so the indifference curves are tangent and the allocation is on the contract curve — Pareto efficient.

  2. In utility space, (u1,u2)=(5,5)(u_1, u_2) = (5, 5)(u1​,u2​)=(5,5), which lies exactly on the utility possibility frontier u2=10−u1u_2 = 10 - u_1u2​=10−u1​ traced along the contract curve (the diagonal). This is the First Welfare Theorem: competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.

Find the lump-sum transfer that decentralizes the Pareto optimum x1=(6,6)x^1 = (6, 6)x1=(6,6), x2=(4,4)x^2 = (4, 4)x2=(4,4) as a competitive equilibrium (Second Welfare Theorem).

p1=MRS1(6,6)=1(supporting price)p_1 = MRS_1(6, 6) = 1 \quad (\text{supporting price})p1​=MRS1​(6,6)=1(supporting price)
T=p⋅(x1−e1)=1⋅(6−7)+(6−3)=2T = p \cdot (x^1 - e^1) = 1 \cdot (6-7) + (6-3) = 2T=p⋅(x1−e1)=1⋅(6−7)+(6−3)=2
Show proof

  1. (6,6)(6, 6)(6,6) is on the diagonal (the contract curve), hence Pareto optimal. The common marginal rate of substitution there is MRS=1MRS = 1MRS=1, so the supporting price is p1=1p_1 = 1p1​=1.

  2. Consumer 1 must afford (6,6)(6, 6)(6,6), requiring wealth 1⋅6+6=121 \cdot 6 + 6 = 121⋅6+6=12.

    Original wealth is w1=10w_1 = 10w1​=10, so a transfer of T=12−10=2T = 12 - 10 = 2T=12−10=2 does it.

    After the transfer, demands are x1=(0.5⋅12, 0.5⋅12)=(6,6)x^1 = (0.5 \cdot 12,\ 0.5 \cdot 12) = (6, 6)x1=(0.5⋅12, 0.5⋅12)=(6,6), x2=(4,4)x^2 = (4, 4)x2=(4,4), and markets clear.
